In Durban, South Africa, a study conducted in 2011 involving 949 clients compared two HIV testing strategies: a serial testing strategy used from March to August 2007, followed by a parallel testing strategy from September to November 2007. In South Korea, 22 patients with negative or discordant rapid HIV test results were found to have positive qualitative HIV RNA test results. Of these, 10 patients were diagnosed with chronic HIV infection. Among 12 patients with discordant rapid test results, 10 were confirmed to have chronic HIV infection through positive enzyme immunoassay (EIA) and/or Western blot (WB) testing. Standard rapid HIV testing missed 2% of patients with chronic HIV infection. 2. In India (2011), 9,419 specimens were tested using HIV rapid tests (Combaids), with positive results further confirmed using Tridot and EIA. Issues such as mislabeling, specimen contamination, and incorrect performance of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) were identified. Discordant results were observed in 50% of cases, with 8% false negatives and 15% incorrect results overall. 3. In Africa (2012), a survey across 30 countries and 49 laboratories highlighted challenges such as insufficient human resources, frequent stockouts of test kits and reagents, and poor uptake of external quality assurance (EQA) schemes. Some sites used only one RDT for HIV diagnosis, deviating from recommended algorithms. Laboratories reported using WHO testing strategies II and III, with the latter employing a third assay platform for confirmation. 4. In Uganda and Tanzania (2012), a pilot program for HIV RDT proficiency testing (PT) was conducted at 200 sites in each country. Training on dried tube specimen (DTS) reconstitution and national HIV testing algorithms was provided. Quarterly PT panels were distributed, and feedback was given to sites with performance scores below 100%. 5. In Kenya (2012), 365 HIV testers were audited due to incorrect PT results. Site visits identified issues such as failure to adhere to national testing algorithms, transcription errors, and poor supervision. On-site mentorship and corrective actions were implemented, with feedback provided directly to testers and facility management. 6. In Tanzania (2012), competency assessments of non-laboratory personnel performing HIV testing were conducted across 26 regions. Testers were evaluated using a panel of 100 proficiency testing samples, and feedback was provided on the same day. Poor performers received retraining on quality assurance procedures. 7. In Zambia and Rwanda (2011), 45,820 clients (tested as couples) were evaluated using up to three sequential RDTs. Discrepant or indeterminate results were observed in 1% of couples, with follow-up testing conducted monthly. Among 661 clients who returned for retesting, 4 false negatives and 17 false positives were identified. 8. In Cambodia (2005), midwives with no prior laboratory experience were trained to perform HIV testing using Determine HIV 1/2 test kits. Laboratory technicians routinely verified test results, and discordant results were retested using the same rapid test kit. 9. In London, UK (2012), a study evaluated the visual interpretation of false-reactive and true-reactive results using Determine HIV 1/2 antibody point-of-care tests (POCT). Independent readers graded line strength from photographs, identifying differences between false and true positives. 10. In Cape Town, South Africa (2010), poor adherence to recommended testing protocols was investigated. Observations of staff administering tests revealed gaps in performance, and testing sensitivity was calculated based on PCR and ELISA results. 11. In Nigeria (2008), a survey of 39 health facilities assessed compliance with national HIV testing algorithms. Structured questionnaires were used to evaluate knowledge, skills, and adherence to protocols. Data analysis revealed gaps in compliance and quality assurance practices. 12. In the Lake Victoria region of Tanzania (2007), a survey of 89 health facilities identified challenges such as the lack of standard operating procedures (SOPs) and unavailability of test kits in some facilities. 13. Across multiple countries in Africa, external quality assessment schemes (EQAS) were established to evaluate the quality of HIV serological testing. Proficiency testing panels were distributed to laboratories, and participation in EQAS was voluntary and free of charge. 14. In India (2011), issues such as mislabeling, specimen contamination, and incorrect RDT performance were reported. Testing discrepancies were observed in 50% of cases, with 8% false negatives and 15% incorrect results overall. 15. In Lusaka, Zambia, and Kigali, Rwanda (2011), research conducted at couples’ voluntary counseling and testing centers revealed that 1% of couples had at least one discrepant or indeterminate rapid test result. Monthly follow-up testing was conducted, with 65% of individuals returning for retesting. 16. In Cambodia (2005), midwives were trained to perform HIV testing using Determine HIV 1/2 test kits. Laboratory technicians verified results, and discordant reports were retested using the same blood samples. 17. In London, UK (2012), a study evaluated the interpretation of rapid HIV test results using photographs. Participants with varying levels of experience scored the results, highlighting differences in technical proficiency. 18. In Nigeria (2006), the government introduced a national HIV testing strategy using five non-cold-chain-dependent rapid test kits. Compliance with these algorithms was evaluated in a survey of health facilities in Abuja, revealing gaps in adherence and quality assurance. 19. In Tanzania (2007), a survey of 89 health facilities identified challenges such as the lack of SOPs and unavailability of test kits in some locations. 20.
